script.scamName: Fake FTC agent phone cutoff call

message.body: FTC: Agent Badge ID 4471-B. A phone registered under your name is being used for scams overseas. Your number will be deactivated unless you cooperate. Do not discuss this case with anyone. A police officer will contact you to file a report.
message.provenanceNote: The FTC Consumer Alert describes this scheme as a phone call from someone claiming to be an FTC official. The call's claims (the badge ID, the phone-registered-in-your-name story, the deactivation threat, the secrecy demand, and the handoff to a fake police officer) are adapted into a text message here so they can be shown on the screen.

evidence.quote: someone claiming to be an FTC official (who’s really a scammer) calls to say a phone was registered under your name and number and is being used to commit scams in another country.
If you don’t cooperate, they threaten to deactivate your phone number.
the FTC impersonator will transfer you to a (fake) police officer to file a report.

script.hook: Real or scam? You get three seconds.
script.stampSay: Scam. The FTC won't cut you off.

flags.label: Phone cutoff threat
flags.say: They scare you by saying your number will be shut off.

evidence.quote: A real FTC employee will never ever threaten to disconnect your phone. That’s a scam.

flags.label: Keep it secret
flags.say: A real FTC employee never tells you to keep your conversations secret.

target.match: Do not discuss this case with anyone

evidence.quote: A real FTC employee will never ever tell you to keep your conversations secret. That’s always a scam.

flags.label: Fake badge number
flags.say: That badge ID is fake and meant to sound official.

evidence.quote: The “FTC official” even reads off their badge ID (it’s a fake badge).

safeMove.label: Report it
safeMove.say: Tell the FTC about it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

evidence.quote: Spot one of these scams? Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

script.title: Fake government agent call says your phone will be cut off
script.description: A caller posing as a government agent says your number is tied to scams and will be shut off. They read off a badge ID and tell you to keep quiet. Here are three signs it is a scam and what to do instead.

message.body: heyyy! ok so I've been making serious money with a crypto trading mentor 🙌 guaranteed 20% returns every week, zero risk. you just send $500 in crypto to open your account. sign up here: crypto-mentor-pro.example
message.provenanceNote: Recreated from the California Attorney General release, which describes a friend's possibly hacked account messaging about a great investment opportunity, guarantees of large returns, and required crypto payments.

evidence.quote: If a friend suddenly messages you about a "great investment opportunity," contact them outside of Facebook via phone call or text to ensure their account hasn't been hacked.
Guarantees of large returns in exchange for money or cryptocurrency: If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
Requiring payments in cryptocurrency: No legitimate companies or government agencies will force you to pay in cryptocurrencies or other crypto assets.

message.body: Blessings family 🙏 Our fund is a registered broker and pays 2 to 4% profit every week. Withdraw your money any time. Earn a bonus for every friend you bring in. Join here: join-tradefund.example
message.provenanceNote: Recreated from the New York Attorney General press release, which describes WhatsApp group chat ads promising two to four percent weekly profits, recruitment bonuses, withdrawals at any time, and false claims of being a registered broker.

evidence.quote: through social media and WhatsApp group chats with fraudulent promises of high returns on investments
advertised high profits from trading of approximately two to four percent per week, promoted recruitment bonuses, and promised that investors could withdraw their funds and profits at any time.

script.hook: This group chat pitch cost thousands their savings.
script.stampSay: It's a pyramid scheme, not an investment.

flags.label: Big weekly profits
flags.say: Group chats like this pushed fraudulent promises of high returns on investments.

evidence.quote: through social media and WhatsApp group chats with fraudulent promises of high returns on investments

flags.label: Paid to recruit
flags.say: This scheme recruited investors with promises of high returns and generous recruitment bonuses.

target.match: a bonus for every friend you bring in

evidence.quote: recruited investors with promises of high returns and generous recruitment bonuses

flags.label: Withdraw anytime claim
flags.say: When the scheme collapsed, tens of thousands could not withdraw their money.

evidence.quote: When NovaTech collapsed in May 2023, tens of thousands of investors were unable to withdraw their cryptocurrency.

safeMove.label: Doubt the license claim
safeMove.say: This fund claimed to be a registered, licensed broker in the U.S., and that was false.

evidence.quote: falsely marketed NovaTech as a registered hedge fund broker, misrepresented that NovaTech was licensed to trade cryptocurrency in the U.S.

message.body:
Sponsored
Open Enrollment is here! Compare health plans, check your coverage, and see if you qualify for savings.
Enroll today at healthcare-gov-enroll.example
Or call (202) 555-0142
message.provenanceNote: Recreated from the FTC Consumer Alerts post, which describes paid ads with lookalike government web addresses, official-looking logos, and a link or phone number inside the ad.

evidence.quote: But before you click on a search result, remember: scammers and dishonest businesses sometimes pay to appear at the top.

Bad actors often use web addresses that look similar to government website addresses. They also use keywords and official-looking logos to make you think you’re at the real Healthcare.gov or Medicare.gov when you’re not.
If you use the link or phone number in the ad, you might end up paying for a scammy plan that’s not health insurance, or expose yourself to medical identity theft.

script.hook: Someone you love sees this ad today.
script.stampSay: A paid ad, not the real site.

flags.label: Paid ad label
flags.say: That small Sponsored tag means someone paid to put this here.

evidence.quote: Look for small “Ad” or “Sponsored” labels next to search results to identify paid ads.

flags.label: Lookalike web address
flags.say: Scammers use web addresses that look a lot like government ones.

evidence.quote: Bad actors often use web addresses that look similar to government website addresses.

flags.label: Number in the ad
flags.say: Call that number and you might pay for a plan that isn't insurance.

evidence.quote: If you use the link or phone number in the ad, you might end up paying for a scammy plan that’s not health insurance, or expose yourself to medical identity theft.

safeMove.label: Type the site yourself
safeMove.say: Skip the ad and type the real website's name into the search engine yourself.

evidence.quote: Type the name of the website directly into the search engine.

script.title: Fake health insurance ad during Open Enrollment
script.description: Paid ads can look like the real government health insurance site. Learn the three signs that an ad is not what it seems. Then see the one safe move to find real plans.

message.body: Transcript: Hi, this is Dana from the Example Charity Fund. Because you donated last year, you were entered in our donor sweepstakes, and you won the $25,000 grand prize! To release the funds, we just need a $299 processing fee and your Social Security number to verify you. Call us back today at (202) 555-0147. Congratulations!
message.provenanceNote: Recreated from the FTC Consumer Alerts article, which describes calls from someone claiming to be with a charity you support, saying you won a sweepstakes and asking you to pay or give your Social Security number. The charity name is clearly fictional and does not refer to any real organization.

evidence.quote: these impersonators sometimes make you believe that you won a charity-sponsored sweepstakes because you’ve donated to that charity.
Only scammers demand you pay or give them personal information like your Social Security number to get a prize.

script.hook: A voicemail says you won. Read it.
script.stampSay: Won a prize? Then why pay?

flags.label: Pay to claim
flags.say: They want money before you get the prize, and that alone means scam.

evidence.quote: The moment someone tells you to pay to claim your prize, you know you’re dealing with a scam.

flags.label: Asks for your Social
flags.say: Only a scammer asks for your Social Security number to hand over a prize.

target.match: Social Security number to verify you

evidence.quote: Only scammers demand you pay or give them personal information like your Social Security number to get a prize.

flags.label: Faked caller ID
flags.say: The name and number on your screen can be faked, so do not trust them.

evidence.quote: Scammers can fake caller ID. Don’t trust it, even if it shows a real government agency or company name or phone number.

safeMove.label: Search, skip the ads
safeMove.say: Search the charity name with the word scam, and scroll past the paid ads first.

evidence.quote: Search online for the name of the contest or company with words like “complaint,” “review,” or “scam” to see what others are saying. But don’t rely on the first search results you see. Sometimes imposters advertise on platforms like Google Search and Bing to lead you to false information. Scroll past the paid ads to help avoid these imposters.

message.subject: Action needed: confirm your login
message.body:
Hello,

We are updating security on the voter records system before the midterm elections. To keep your access, please confirm your login details.

Confirm your login: https://voter-portal-login.example/verify

Thank you,
County Election Office IT Team
message.provenanceNote: Recreated from the FBI IC3 PSA, which describes phishing emails that closely resemble legitimate communications and try to get election and campaign officials to disclose login credentials.

evidence.quote: these actors have crafted increasingly sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications, making it difficult for targets to distinguish fraudulent messages
Malicious cyber actors may attempt to disrupt the 2026 U.S. midterm elections using phishing and smishing techniques to steal user data, including login credentials and sensitive information.

script.hook: Would you tap this election office email?
script.stampSay: A fake made to steal your login.

flags.label: Wants your login
flags.say: Phishing messages try to trick you into handing over your login details.

evidence.quote: phishing and smishing attempts that try to manipulate the recipient into disclosing sensitive information, such as login credentials or financial information

flags.label: No typos, still fake
flags.say: Scammers now use smart tools to write messages that sound real and natural.

target.match: We are updating security on the voter records system

evidence.quote: SI allows malicious cyber actors to create language that appears genuine, using native languages and common vernacular, making it more likely for potential victims to click malicious links

flags.label: Out of the blue
flags.say: Be careful when a request for login details shows up that you never asked for.

evidence.quote: Advise employees to be cautious when providing sensitive information — such as login credentials — electronically or over the phone, particularly if unsolicited or anomalous.

safeMove.label: Check another way
safeMove.say: Confirm any request for login details through a separate channel before you share anything.

evidence.quote: Employees should confirm, if possible, requests for sensitive information through secondary channels.

skipped.reason: problems: The 'Badge photo proof' flag targets an attachment, but the message has none. The body only states a badge ID number in text. The flag points at nothing on screen.

problems: Flag 1 'say' ('No real investment hands you a set profit every single week') is a general claim about all legitimate investments. The quote only says NovaTech advertised about 2-4% per week. The source never says fixed weekly returns are impossible for real investments.

problems: Flag 'Friendly mentor': the say line 'then drain everything' is not supported by the attached quote, which only covers mentors building trust. The source does say scammers 'ultimately vanish with all the victim's money,' but that line is not the cited evidence. Either swap the quote or soften the say line.

problems: provenanceNote says the source describes a follow-up text with a fake employee ID photo 'that the source says scammers send.' The source never says scammers in this scheme text a photo. It only says a real FTC employee will never text a photo of their employee ID. In the source, the badge ID is read aloud on the call. The note should not attribute this to the source.

problems: The 'Faith used as bait' flag targets the sender with an empty match string, so it highlights nothing specific. The religious appeal is in the body ('God has opened a door for us'), so the flag should target that text.
problems: Flag 'Friendly stranger mentor' has target kind 'sender' with an empty match string, so it does not point at the sender 'Coach Daniel'.
problems: safeMove label 'Keep your crypto' is advice the source never gives. The source only reports that investors could not withdraw when NovaTech collapsed; it offers no protective guidance.
